Basically each state has a number of "delegates" that are awarded to a candidate based on the popular vote percentage they won in that state's primary/caucus. You add up all the delegates after all 50 states have voted and the winner gets to be that party's candidate for president.

Superdelegates make up about 15% of total delegates and may support whoever they want regardless of popular vote. These are mayors, senators, etc that represent the interests of the party.

Hillary has most superdelegates support today because she is the establishment candidate. They can still change their minds. However they really don't matter! Superdelegates have never been able to stomp on the popular vote. Whoever gets the popular vote gets the candidacy.

The big parties in the United States are the Republicans and Democrats. Their primaries are the ones you'll see on the news. Third (minor) parties are often barred from holding primaries in some states. Members of the general public can participate in a party's state primary if they are (1) of voting age and (2) registered with the party in question (or registered as an independent in states that allow independents to vote in party primaries). Superdelegates are elected officials or party officials in the Democratic Party that get to vote as delegates in the primary, with the same power as delegates chosen by a vote of party members. The Republicans have a similar category of delegates. The category of superdelegates (unpledged) and pledged delegates arose in the Democratic Party after the riots in 1968, which is really too complex to go into here.
